replacement.objective: Avoid duplicating a teammate’s pressure without checking coverage.
replacement.briefing: D1 pressures Gold 1 in the puck-side corner. YOU are near the net front. Gold 2 is in the slot. The coach’s stated plan has D1 contesting the corner while YOU protect the inside threat. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.

questions.prompt: Where is the off-puck attacker Gold 2?

options.text: At the attacking blue line on the right

questions.explanation: Gold 2 is central in the defending zone, nearer the slot than either wall.

questions.prompt: Choose two checks before joining the corner.

options.text: Whether two defenders near every puck is always better

questions.explanation: Extra puck pressure can leave another threat; the stated assignment matters.

questions.prompt: Arrange a read before leaving the net front.
questions.explanation: This follows the exercise’s coverage plan, not a universal requirement for every defensive system.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare another inside position between Gold 2 and the net.
questions.explanation: This keeps a net-side relationship while retaining a possible view of the corner. Other coverage shapes may differ.

questions.prompt: D1 falls and Gold 1 gains a path toward the net. What changes?

options.text: Treat the old corner assignment as unchangeable
Leave Gold 1’s new path out of the read
Reassess the immediate puck threat and coordinate coverage

questions.explanation: A new immediate threat can require an adjustment; the scenario does not dictate a universal switch.

questions.prompt: How could both defenders chasing the corner make Gold 1’s job easier?
questions.explanation: Gold 1 may gain a pass to Gold 2 or open inside ice. Explain the tradeoff rather than saying support is always wrong.

questions.prompt: Which Navy teammate’s corner pressure should YOU confirm before leaving the net front?
questions.explanation: D1 is the Navy defender assigned to contest Gold 1 in the corner, so YOU can leave only after checking that pressure and Gold 2’s inside route; if D1 falls, stay net-side.

questions.prompt: Which two checks precede leaving the net front?
questions.explanation: D1’s pressure and Gold 2’s net-side route tell YOU whether leaving helps; corner activity alone does not.

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to the lane between Gold 2 and the Navy net.
questions.explanation: The inside position protects the slot while D1 contests the corner; if Gold 1 wins inside, switch to that carrier.

questions.prompt: If YOU decide to leave the net front, what should YOU communicate to D1 before making the move?
questions.explanation: A short call — such as confirming D1 has Gold 1 contained, or telling D1 that YOU are stepping away from the net front — helps D1 adjust instead of being surprised. There is no single required wording, and what YOU say can change with what D1 signals back.
